extracted.intended_audience: researchers submitting to or reviewing for eLife; journal editors and referees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance describing eLife's editorial and peer-review workflow and the standards reviewers and editors should apply when evaluating life/biomedical science manuscripts, emphasizing fairness, speed and transparency. Covers initial triage, reviewer behavior, consultation, decision letters, revision handling, and transparency practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial authority by working scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: All editorial decisions at eLife are taken by working scientists in the research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign authority for editorial decisions to active researchers (senior editors and members of the Board of Reviewing Editors) to ensure judgments are decisive and fair; editors are remunerated in recognition of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial triage and assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paper is submitted it is assigned to one of the senior editors who makes the initial decision, usually after consulting colleagues and BRE members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are asked at submission to identify appropriate editors and propose referees, and may request exclusion of certain editors/referees. Approximately 43% of initial submissions pass this stage; median time to initial decision about three days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance threshold for full submission
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work is judged to represent a significant achievement using a broad set of criteria, a full submission is encouraged and a reviewing editor is appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewing editor is chosen from the BRE or senior editors and will act as a referee, select additional referees, and oversee the peer review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit recommendations to changes bearing on major conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are directed to limit their recommendations to changes that bear directly on the major conclusions of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly: 'We will only request new work, such as experiments, analyses, or data collection, if the data are essential to support the major conclusions.' Additional guidance: authors must be able to do any new work in a reasonable time frame; any requests for new work must fall within the scope of the current submission and the technical expertise of the authors; if conclusions are not adequately supported by existing data, the submission should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer consultation to reach consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: After reviews are received the reviewing editor initiates an online consultation session in which each referee can see who the other referees are and what they wrote, and referees exchange views over several days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation is intended to allow referees to discuss merits collectively and reach a consensus on acceptance, revision, or rejection; the process has been found to be engaging and to improve on anonymous isolated reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey full reviews on rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the consensus is that the manuscript should be rejected, the reviews are usually conveyed to the authors in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides authors with detailed rationale when the decision is unfavorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision letters to summarize essential revisions concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: If the consensus is that the manuscript is, in principle, acceptable but requires additional experiments or analysis, referees work together to identify the additional studies required and the reviewing editor drafts a decision letter that explains these essential revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial preference is that core comments be summarized in at most 1000 words. Concision is emphasized: only include concerns that affect validity or overall conclusions in the decision letter; other concerns may be conveyed but must be clearly indicated as non-essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude non-essential concerns from required revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that do not affect the validity or overall conclusions of the manuscript are not included in the decision letter as required revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such concerns may sometimes be conveyed to authors but must be clearly labelled as not essential to acceptance, avoiding unnecessary demands on authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and approval of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: All decisions, either favourable or unfavourable, are reviewed and approved by the Editor-in-Chief or a Deputy Editor, plus one other senior editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an additional layer of quality control over the outcome of peer review and ensures consistency across decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving deadlock and confidentiality in consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a consensus cannot be reached the relevant senior editor can be called on to make a final decision; referees see each other's identities and reports during consultation, while confidentiality can be maintained where desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consultation model aims to enable junior referees to express contrary views without intimidation; confidentiality and the senior-editor tie-breaker are protections built into the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive decision on revised manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When the revised manuscript is received the reviewing editor can usually make an executive decision on whether the authors have addressed the major concerns in a satisfactory manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows faster final decisions and contributes to a shorter median time from full submission to acceptance (reported under 80 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: publish decision letter and author response
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to approval by the authors, the decision letter after peer review and the author response are included in the HTML version of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of decision letters and responses is part of eLife's commitment to making the peer review process more transparent and informative to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, speed and transparency as guiding principles
rubrics_metrics.description: eLife emphasizes fairness, speed and transparency in editorial judgments and the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles motivate process choices such as active-scientist editors, reviewer consultation, concise decision letters, limited requests for new work, and publishing decision correspondence.
